impertinent

/im-PER-tuh-nent/ — stress on second syllable; rhymes with pertinent · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Someone who is impertinent is rude or disrespectful, especially by speaking or acting toward others with inappropriate boldness.

Asking the judge her age was an impertinent question that silenced the courtroom.

Example

A student stands up in a job interview and asks the CEO an impertinent question: why does the company pay its executives so much more than minimum-wage workers?

The question is not just rude—it crosses a line. The student is inappropriately bold, asking something that oversteps the bounds of what is fitting for a job interview. Impertinent captures the rudeness combined with the sense of 'you should not have said that.' A word like 'rude' would miss the 'out of place' part that makes impertinence distinct.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

disrespectful: Disrespectful means failing to give someone the respect they are owed — a broad label for any slight, deliberate or careless. Impertinent is narrower and bolder: a remark or question that oversteps what the speaker had any place to say. Every impertinent remark is disrespectful, but only the boldly out-of-place ones are impertinent.

presumptuous: Presumptuous means assuming a right, role, or outcome that is not yet yours to claim — acting as if permission had already been granted. Impertinent oversteps in speech instead: a bold, prying remark aimed at someone, beyond what the speaker has any business saying. Presumption grabs a privilege; impertinence talks out of turn.

impudent: Impudent means boldly disrespectful with a shameless, cocky edge — the impudent speaker enjoys the daring and shows no embarrassment. Impertinent stresses something different: the remark is out of place, overstepping what the moment or the speaker's position allows. Impudence is about nerve; impertinence is about crossing a line.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

courteous: consistently polite and considerate toward others

tactful: careful to speak without giving offense

Where it sits · how deliberately the words offend

thoughtless → rude → impertinent → insulting

thoughtless vs. impertinent: Thoughtless is much weaker than impertinent: a thoughtless remark offends by accident, while an impertinent remark boldly oversteps what the speaker has any place to say.

rude vs. impertinent: Rude is weaker than impertinent; rude covers bad manners in general, but impertinent points to a specific bold remark or question that goes beyond its proper place.

insulting vs. impertinent: Insulting is stronger than impertinent: an impertinent question oversteps the bounds of politeness, while an insulting one is deliberately meant to wound or demean.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — im-: not, opposite of (form of in-) (Latin)

Root — pertin (pertinere): to belong, to be relevant (per 'through' + tenere 'to hold') (Latin)

Suffix — -ent: forming adjectives: doing or being (Latin)

Put it together: Impertinent literally means 'not belonging, not to the point.' An impertinent remark is one that doesn't belong — a question or comment that boldly steps outside its proper place, which is exactly why it strikes people as rude.

Use the root in a new word: pertinent: The lawyer kept only the pertinent files — the ones that truly belonged to the case — while an impertinent question is literally one that does 'not belong' where it is asked.

Strength Check

Word Choice

formal / literary

Impertinent is stronger than rude because it emphasizes that someone is being disrespectful in a way that is inappropriate for the situation—overstepping boundaries. Use it when someone speaks or acts boldly out of place. For basic rudeness, rude is the simpler choice.
